unit.title: Orders
unit.description: Market, limit, stop loss, take profit and OCO: which order to use and what it costs

texts: Buy and sell straight away
This is a big, heavily traded share. You buy 100 and, a second later, change your mind.
You **sell them straight away**. What happens?
You break even
You lose about €2
You make a little
You buy at €10.02, what sellers are asking (*ask*), and sell at €10.00, what buyers are paying (*bid*): you lose **€2**, 0.2 %.
Buy so much that slippage costs more than the spread (0.2 %).

That gap between *ask* and *bid* is the **spread**: you lose it when you buy and sell straight away. If you buy a lot, you also pay **slippage**: the difference between the price you expected and the price you get.
Now slippage costs you more than the spread.
The first step of the book isn't enough any more.
Look at the spread, then raise the quantity
«Zero fees»
Pablo
My broker charges 0 fees. I make 20 trades of €1,000 a month.
Between the spread and everything else, each one costs me 0.3 %. Nothing.
Is trading like this free for him?
Yes: his broker charges no fees
He still pays the spread: he buys at the ask and sells at the bid.
Almost: 0.3 % is very little
That's €3 per trade: **€720** in a year.
No: he'll pay a lot, win or lose
That's it: €3 × 20 × 12 months = **€720** a year.
Ugh… so what do I do?
Trade less. Costs are the only certain thing about an investment.

steps.title: When there's more slippage
steps.body:
When your order is large for the book or the price is moving very fast: at the **open**, after **news** or in moments of **panic**.

The more **liquidity**, the narrower the spread. As a percentage, spread ÷ price: €10.00 / €10.02 is 0.2 %.
steps.key: Spread, slippage and fees are trading costs: the more you trade, the more you pay.
steps.tip: Try it: before buying in Market, check the simulated fee on your order.

texts: Does it execute?
A share trades at €50 and you only want it at €47. With a **limit order** you set the price: you buy at your price **or cheaper** and sell at your price **or higher**.
It executes
It doesn't execute
Buy limit at €47. The day's low is €47.40
The price didn't reach your limit: the order keeps waiting (or expires, if it was a day order).
Buy limit at €47. The price drops to €46.80
It reaches your limit: you buy at €47 or better.
Sell limit at €60. Someone pays €60.30
It sells at your price or better: if someone pays more, all the better for you.
Sell limit at €60. The day's high is €59.50
It didn't reach your price: you don't sell.
Buy limit at €52 with the share at €50
Above the current price it executes straight away, at the best price available.
A «day» limit order that doesn't reach its price
It expires at the close without executing.
Decide what happens to the six orders.
**Limit order = guaranteed price, no guaranteed execution.** If the price doesn't reach your limit, it doesn't execute, or only partly executes.
Hint: a buy fills at your price or lower; a sell, at your price or higher.
See? You set the price, the market decides whether it gets there.
Does it execute or not? Tap each order
The forgotten order
Leo
A month ago I placed a «good till cancelled» buy limit. I'd totally forgotten.
Today it executed, right after some terrible news!
What do you tell Leo?
Great: you bought cheap
Maybe, but he bought without deciding to today, with new information.
Check your live orders now and then
Exactly. A live order doesn't know the news has changed.
Always use day orders
They expire at the close, yes. But good-till-cancelled ones are useful if you check them.
Many brokers put a limit on them, often 90 days.

steps.title: When to use it
steps.body:
When the price matters to you: illiquid securities, wide spreads, the open, or if you only want to buy in a specific zone.

**Duration:** day (it expires at the close) or good till cancelled (*GTC*), which stays live until it's filled or you cancel it.
steps.key: With a limit order you control the price; in exchange, it may never execute.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, set a price alert where you'd put your limit order.

texts: Your emergency exit
You buy Tesla at the last price and go to bed. A **stop loss** is a sleeping order: it only wakes up if the price **falls to the level** you choose.
The price falls to your stop while you're asleep. What does the order do?
It alerts you so you can decide
It sells by itself, at whatever price there is at that moment
It sells exactly at the stop price, guaranteed
When the level is touched, the stop becomes a **market** order: it sells at the best available price, without asking you.
Set a stop and a target and see which of the two orders gets executed.
The stop doesn't warn or ask: **it sells by itself** when the price touches its level. Where to put it so that noise doesn't trigger it is something you'll see in «Risk management».
It hit your target before the stop: the sale went through at a gain.
The stop was triggered: the order sold by itself.
Move the stop and hit «See what happened»
The stop that didn't sell
Sara
I bought at €20 and set a **stop-limit**: if it touches €18, sell, but not for less than €17.80.
Bad news before the open. The share opens straight at **€16.50**.
What happens to her order?
It sells at €18
At €18 there are no buyers left: the price has jumped below it.
It's triggered, but it doesn't sell: nobody pays €17.80
That's it. Her limit order sits there waiting, and Sara is still in while it falls.
It sells at €16.50
That's what would have happened with a market stop. With the stop-limit, it won't sell below €17.80.
So with a market stop I'd have sold at €16.50?
Yes: worse than planned, but out. **A market stop gets you out for sure; a stop-limit controls the price, but you may not get out.**

steps.title: Before you leave it in place
steps.body:
• **Validity:** a «day» stop expires at the close. For it to still be there tomorrow, choose «good till cancelled».
• **Gaps:** if the price opens below your level, a market stop sells at the first price available.
• **It doesn't move away:** you decide the stop before you enter, with a cool head.

How much to buy so that this loss stays small is something you learn in «Risk management».
steps.key: A stop is a sleeping order that sells by itself when the price touches its level.
steps.tip: Pass this lesson and add a stop loss to your next purchase in Market.

texts: Set your target
You buy Ethereum at the last price and don't want to spend all day watching. A **take profit** will sell only if the price **rises to your target**.
Your target is **15 %** up, way above the previous high. What do you think?
It'll get hit: crypto moves a lot
It might never get hit
It's bound to get hit: you just have to wait
The previous high is **10.7 %** up: lots of people sold there and selling tends to show up again.
Put the target where the price can get to and see whether it's executed.
At 15 %, the target isn't hit in these candles (they end at +5.5 %); **near the previous high**, it is. A take profit is a **limit sell order**: if the price doesn't get there, it isn't executed.
Target hit! The sale happened on its own.
The stop was triggered. Put it below the last low.
Neither stop nor target. What if you move it closer to the previous high?
Place the target and hit «See what happened»
It sold… and kept going up
Laura
I bought at €30 with my target at €36. It sold in three weeks.
A week later it's trading at €39. So annoying!
What do you tell Laura?
She stuck to her plan: she made 20 %
Exactly. A good plan doesn't catch the top: it protects what you make.
Check whether her target was reasonable
Fine, but without beating herself up: she made 20 % by following her plan.
Buy back in right now, at €39
Buying out of frustration isn't a plan: it's a reaction.
Whatever it rises after your target isn't yours any more.
That's the price of having a plan. Decide your target before you get in.

steps.title: What a take profit does
steps.body:
It's a **limit sell order** above the price: it sells by itself if the price rises to your target.

• If the price **doesn't get there**, it isn't executed and you stay in.
• Like any order, it has a **validity**: day or good till cancelled.
• You decide it **before you enter**, not once you're already winning.

How much it's worth making for each euro you risk is something you learn in «Risk management».
steps.key: The take profit gets you out at the top; the stop, at the bottom.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next purchase in Market, add a take profit near the previous high.

texts: Set up your OCO
You're going away for a week and won't be able to check the price. An **OCO** pairs a stop below with a target above: **when one is triggered, the other cancels itself.**
Put the stop below the last low and the target near the previous high, and see what gets triggered.
An OCO is a complete exit plan: **when one order is triggered, the other cancels itself**. You're not left with any stray orders.
The stop was triggered: the target cancelled itself.
Target hit: the stop cancelled itself.
Neither was triggered: both are still live.
Place the stop and the target, and hit «See what happened»
The gap
Pablo
I bought at €40. I've got an OCO with the stop at €38.
Overnight, the company reports bad results. It opens at €34.
Roughly what price does Pablo sell at?
€38, his stop
There were no prices between €38 and €34: it's a **gap**.
Around €34
Exactly. The stop sells at the first available price.
He doesn't sell: the price jumped over the stop
He does sell, but at the first price there is: about €34.
What about my target?
It cancels itself. But no stop is perfect insurance.
Against gaps, your best defence is the **size** of your position.

steps.title: The trailing stop
steps.body:
A **trailing stop** rises with the price at a fixed distance: at 8 %, if the price goes from €100 to €120, your stop rises from €92 to €110.40. It never goes down.

Gaps happen on the way up too: if it opens above your target, the take profit executes at that price, better than expected.

Not every broker offers OCO orders: check first.
steps.key: OCO = complete exit plan; gaps are its limit.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, set a stop and a take profit on the same purchase.

u6l2-5.prompt: What usually has the smallest spread?
u6l2-5.explanation: The more liquidity, the narrower the spread.

u6l2-6.prompt: Match each cost with its definition.
u6l2-6.explanation: The first three are costs; liquidity is what keeps them low.
right: Difference between the expected price and the one you get
What the broker charges for trading
Being able to trade a lot without moving the price
Difference between bid and ask

u6l2-9.prompt: When is there usually more slippage? Select all that apply.
options: With large orders in illiquid securities
With a small order in a big company mid-session
In moments of panic, with the price moving very fast
With a limit order that fixes your price
u6l2-9.explanation: Slippage shows up when liquidity is thin or the price is racing: large orders in illiquid securities, moments of panic, opens after news. A limit order fixes your price.

u6l2-10.prompt: Marta wants to buy €3,000 of a small company with a 1 % spread. What does she do?
options: Buys at market and sells as soon as she's slightly up
Uses a limit order and rarely trades that stock
Buys and sells several times a day to catch the moves
u6l2-10.explanation: With high-spread securities, trading a lot is a sure way to lose money.
feedback: She needs it to rise more than 1 % just to cover the spread.
She controls her entry price and doesn't pay that 1 % over and over.
Every round trip costs her 1 %: the spread eats up any gain.

u6l3-1.prompt: You want to buy, but only if the price drops to €45. Which order do you use?
options: Market order, when it falls to €45
u6l3-1.explanation: The limit order only executes at €45 or less.

u6l3-4.prompt: You hold shares bought at the last price. Place a sell limit order at a level with a real chance of executing.
u6l3-4.explanation: Selling tends to show up near the previous high: it's a reasonable target. Much higher up, the order may never execute.

u6l3-5.prompt: You're buying with a €5,000 portfolio and risking 2 % at most (€100). Set the stop and choose how much to invest.
u6l3-5.explanation: The amount comes from the stop: with a stop further away you buy less so you don't go over €100 of risk.

u6l3-6.prompt: Ana wants 1,000 shares of an illiquid stock: the best seller is asking €8.40 but only for 100 shares, and the next ones are asking €8.90. What does she do?
options: Buy limit at €9.50, to be sure
u6l3-6.explanation: A useful limit sits close to the price you actually want to pay.
feedback: She buys whatever's there up to €8.45 and the rest waits. She doesn't pay €8.90 by surprise.
She eats through the book: 100 at €8.40 and 900 at €8.90 or more.
That doesn't limit anything: it would execute almost like a market order.

u6l3-8.prompt: Match each order with what it does.
u6l3-8.explanation: Limit price and duration: the two things you choose in a limit order.
right: At your price or higher
Expires at the close
Stays live until filled or you cancel it
At your price or cheaper

u6l4-1.prompt: You've bought at the last price. Place the stop loss where your idea stops being valid.
u6l4-1.explanation: Just below the last meaningful low: if it breaks that, the rise you expected is no longer on.

u6l4-6.prompt: Where does a stop loss make most sense?
options: A few cents from the purchase price, to lose little
u6l4-6.explanation: That's where your idea stops being valid; too close, and normal noise knocks you out for no reason.

u6l4-9.prompt: Match each case with what happens.
u6l4-9.explanation: There's no perfect stop: every option has its cost.
right: Controls the price, but may not execute
Normal noise knocks you out
You don't know how much you could lose
Sure to get out, maybe at a worse price

u6l5-1.prompt: You've bought at the last price. Place your target (take profit) somewhere logical.
u6l5-1.explanation: Near the previous high: it's where lots of people sold and selling tends to show up again.

u6l5-2.prompt: Another trade: place the take profit.
u6l5-2.explanation: Near the previous high, without overdoing it: an overambitious target may never be hit.

u6l5-10.prompt: What does a take profit do? Select all that apply.
options: Protects you if the price falls
Locks in the gain if the target is reached
u6l5-10.explanation: The take profit sells by itself, without you watching, and locks in the gain if the target is reached. It doesn't guarantee selling at the top, and it's the stop, not the take profit, that protects you from falls.

u6l6-1.prompt: Build your OCO. First, place the stop loss.
u6l6-1.explanation: Below the recent low: if it breaks that, your idea no longer holds.

u6l6-2.prompt: Now, in the same trade, place the take profit.
u6l6-2.explanation: Near the previous high. With stop and target in place, the OCO cancels one when the other is triggered.

u6l6-3.prompt: Put in order what happens with an OCO that ends at the target.
options: You place the stop and the target as an OCO
The price rises to the target
u6l6-3.explanation: One executes and the other disappears: you're not left with a stray order.

u6l6-5.prompt: Bruno is going to hold some shares through the company's results day and knows there could be a gap. What does he do?
options: Trusts that the stop will definitely protect him
Cuts the size of the position
Doubles the position because he has a stop
u6l6-5.explanation: Against gaps, the best defence is position size.
feedback: With a gap, the stop executes well below its level.
If it gaps, he loses more per share than planned, but on a small position.
Double the size and a stop that doesn't protect against gaps: a double blow.

u6l6-10.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
u6l6-10.explanation: Combined orders automate your plan, but they don't get rid of gaps.
right: Price jump with no trades in between
Rises with the price and never falls
May not execute if the price jumps
Stop and target: one cancels the other

options: A thinly traded share right at the open
A small company on BME Growth
u6l2-11.explanation: Where there are lots of buyers and sellers, the spread is narrow. With little liquidity, or at the open, it widens: that's why small, thinly traded things cost more to trade.
right: Narrow
Wide

u6l2-12.prompt: Lumi thinks that with a 0-commission broker, buying and selling every day is free. What do you say?
options: No: every buy and every sell pays the spread
You only pay if you lose money
Exactly: if the broker charges no fee, trading costs nothing
u6l2-12.explanation: «0 fees» isn't free: spread and slippage are always paid, and they multiply with every trade.
feedback: That's it! Trading costs add up on every trade, win or lose.
Costs are paid on every trade, including the ones you win.
Every round trip pays the spread: you buy at the ask and sell at the bid, whether or not the broker charges a fee.
lines: My broker charges 0 fees: I can buy and sell every day for free, right?

u6l5-11.prompt: Lumi wants to set her target 50 % above the price to make more. What do you say?
options: Better not to set a target and sell by eye
Good idea: the further away, the more you make
u6l5-11.explanation: The distant target looks like it makes more, but if it's never hit it makes nothing. Selling tends to appear near the previous high, and there the target has a real chance.
feedback: That's it! A reasonable target gets hit more often: making a bit less, but for real.
Without a target, greed or fear decide, right at the worst moment.
Only if it gets there. A target that's too far away may never be hit and end up at the stop.
lines: I'll set my target 50 % higher: that way, when it gets there, I make much more

u6l4-11.prompt: You have a market stop at €30. The share closes at €31 and opens the next day at €27. At what price do you sell?
feedback: A market stop is executed as long as there are buyers.
The stop doesn't guarantee the price: no trade took place at €30.
That's it: the stop is triggered at the open and sells at market.
u6l4-11.explanation: With a gap, a market stop sells at the first available price, which may be worse than your level.

u6l4-12.prompt: Is it typical of a market stop or of a stop-limit?
options: The selling price may be worse than planned
You set the worst price you'll accept
It sells for sure when the level is touched
right: Market stop
Stop-limit
u6l4-12.explanation: A market stop gets you out for sure; a stop-limit controls the price, but you may not get out.

u6l4-13.prompt: You set a «day» stop and the price doesn't touch it. What happens at the close?
options: It expires: tomorrow you have no stop
It turns into a market order at the close
u6l4-13.explanation: A day order expires at the close. For it to stay in place, choose «good till cancelled».

u6l5-13.prompt: Your take profit is at €36, valid «for the day». The price rises to €35.90 and the session closes. What happens?
options: It sells tomorrow, when it touches €36
u6l5-13.explanation: A limit sell order is only executed at its price or better. And if it was a day order, tomorrow it's no longer there.

options: It sits below the purchase price
It sits above the purchase price
When triggered, it sells at market
right: Take profit
Stop loss
u6l5-14.explanation: The take profit gets you out at the top, with a limit order; the stop, at the bottom, at market.
